turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Well, I'm here because... I just can't stop focusing on how I look. Mostly my hairline, and just the way my face looks. I work as a host at a restaurant, and under those lights, I just look really old and... strange. It takes up all my thoughts. My coworkers keep telling me they don't see what I'm talking about, but I know what I see, and I just can't stop thinking about it.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient explicitly states an obsessive preoccupation with perceived flaws in their hairline and facial appearance that take up all their thoughts, despite coworkers reporting they do not see any issue.

turns.doctor_question: When you're thinking about your appearance, do you find yourself doing anything repetitive with your hair or skin, like pulling out hairs, picking at your skin, or anything like that?
turns.patient_response:
No, I don't really pick at my skin or pull my hair out. But I do repeat other things. Like, right before a shift, I just keep checking the bathroom mirror. I'll take pictures on my phone from all these different angles to see how bad it looks, and I spend a lot of time just combing my hair forward, trying to hide it. 

I also just keep replaying in my head exactly how the guests might see me when they walk in. I do it over and over until I'm either late for work, or I just get too worked up to even go out to the front stand.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient confirms performing repetitive behaviors and mental acts regarding their appearance, including repeated mirror checking, taking photos to inspect flaws, camouflaging their hair, and mentally rehearsing how others perceive them.

turns.doctor_question: When you look in the mirror and see these problems with your hairline and face, do you think most people would notice these same flaws if they looked at you, or do you think this might be something that's mostly noticeable to you?
turns.patient_response:
I honestly don't know for sure. Like I said earlier, my coworkers tell me they don't see what I'm talking about. But... when I look in the mirror, it's just so obvious to me. 

It feels like every customer walking into the restaurant must be staring right at my hairline and how old my face looks. So, I guess I'm not entirely sure if strangers actually notice it as much as I do, or if it's mostly just me. I just know what I see, and it's hard not to feel like everyone else must be seeing it too.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes perceived flaws in their hairline and aging face that coworkers say they cannot see, illustrating preoccupation with appearance flaws not observable to others.

turns.doctor_question: When you really think about it logically, do you believe that your hairline and face are actually as noticeable and problematic as your mind tells you they are, or do you suspect that your concern might be out of proportion to how others actually perceive you?

I'm not really sure how to answer that. I try to think about it logically, but... it's hard. I hear what my coworkers say, so maybe part of me wonders if I'm making it a bigger deal than it is. 

But then I look in the mirror, and it's just right there. It feels so real to me. So I really don't know if my concern is out of proportion or not. I just know how bad it looks to me, and it's really hard to get past that, no matter how much I try to rationalize it.

turns.doctor_question: When you think about what your coworkers are telling you—that they don't see these flaws—does any part of you believe they might actually be right, or are you pretty convinced that they're just being nice or not looking closely enough?

I really couldn't tell you. Um... sometimes I think they're just being polite, you know, because we have to work together every day. Or maybe they just aren't looking that closely since the lighting in the restaurant is kind of dim and we're usually rushing around. 

But I can't say for sure. I don't know if they actually mean it when they say I look fine, or if they're just humoring me to get me to stop talking about it. I just really don't know what to believe anymore.

turns.doctor_question: If you were to step back and think about it from a completely neutral perspective, do you think it's possible that your concern about your hairline and face might be more intense than what most other people would feel about similar minor changes to their appearance?

turns.doctor_question: When your coworkers tell you they don't see these flaws you're describing, does any part of you think there's a real possibility they might actually be telling you the truth, or do you feel fairly certain that what you see in the mirror is definitely real regardless of what they say?

turns.doctor_question: When you hear your coworkers say they don't see these flaws, and you think about how consistently they've all said the same thing, does any part of you wonder if maybe your eyes or your brain might be showing you something that isn't actually as bad as it seems—even if you can't quite believe it?
